3559.heavy: For primary stress: CVV only, i.e. phonemic long vowels and rhythmically lengthened vowels (the second in a sequence of nonfinal open syllables); CVC counts as light for primary stress. For secondary stress: CVV and CVC. Three-way hierarchy CVV > CVC > CV; all final syllables are stressed regardless of weight.

3559.prule: Primary stress falls on the CVV syllable (phonemic long vowel or rhythmically lengthened vowel) if the word contains one, in any position; in words with no CVV it falls on the final syllable, even a final CV after a nonfinal CVC. In words with two or more CVV the location of primary stress varies freely between and within speakers (first CVV, second CVV, or both; Gordon 2005 states it as the rightmost long or lengthened vowel).
3559.srule: All heavy syllables (CVC and CVV, CVV including phonemic long vowels and the rhythmically lengthened second vowel of a nonfinal CV.CV sequence) and every word-final syllable (even a final CV after another stress) are stressed; a nonfinal light CV is stressed only as the second member of a light pair (left-to-right iambs). Those stressed syllables that do not bear the primary stress carry secondary stress.
3559.quote: The location of stress is phonologically predictable, falling on word-final syllables, heavy (CVC and CVV) syllables, and on the second in a sequence of light (CV) syllables. 3559.tone: Not a tone language. A morpholexical pitch-accent system ('grades') coexists with stress: 'A subset of verbs is marked as carrying a pitch accent, phonetically a high tone, on a particular syllable' (Gordon 2004 sec. 2.3, p. 5); JIPA 2001 p. 289: 'Although Chickasaw is not a tonal language, in certain morphological forms termed grades there is often a syllable in the word which receives a high pitch accent'. Gordon 2004 concludes that stress exists in addition to the pitch accents and that Chickasaw is a stress-accent language at the word level (p. 24). IP-final words carry a phrasal nuclear pitch accent (final syllable in statements; final CVV, else heavy penult, else antepenult in questions).

3560.prule: Stress falls on the stem syllable of the content word. Every content word is an obligatory monosyllabic person/TAM/possessor prefix plus a (monosyllabic) stem, optionally plus suffixes, so the stem is the second syllable of the word in every example given (su.pã́.me 'he doesn't know', su.sa.bú.me 'he does not teach them', nam.bá.ɾó̃ 'my hat', kám.bĩrk' 'you are a thief'); suffixes that add syllables do not attract stress ('the stressed stem syllable'). Correlates: longer vowel duration and higher intensity (attributed to Herrera 2014); glottal consonants, breathy/creaky vowels and the full phonemic inventory are restricted to the stressed stem syllable.

tn.quote: As already mentioned above, Chichimeco is a tone language. There are two level tones, high and low, and sandhi phenomena have not been noted. Tone can have a lexical as well as a grammatical function. It is extensively used to distinguish the persons in verbs and nouns. Most commonly, the second person verb or noun has a different tone than the first and third person. ... Considering examples given in the literature, it seems that any syllable can carry either tone, at least in the minimal content word, i.e. prefix + stem.

3562.dq: Acento de intensidad: en la primera sílaba de la última raíz de una palabra
3562.dloc: §2.2 'Los sistemas fonológicos del español y del zapoteco', example (5), p. 18.
3562.prule: Dynamic stress ('acento de intensidad') falls on the first syllable of the last (rightmost) root of the word; prefixes, including lexical prefixes, do not take stress. The author states the position is not predictable in phonological terms because roots are one or two syllables in native words (more in loans) and may carry unstressed lexical prefixes; the position is fixed by the morphological parse, not by syllable count or weight.
3562.quote: Tono: grave (sin marca), ascendente (´) y descendente (^), señalados con el diacrítico correspondiente sobre la vocal que porta el tono Acento de intensidad: en la primera sílaba de la última raíz de una palabra; no es predecible en términos fonológicos puesto que una raíz puede tener una o dos sílabas en palabras nativas –más en préstamos– y puede llevar prefijos léxicos que no aceptan el acento (un signo de más, +, aparece antes de la sílaba tónica en los ejemplos cuando el acento no recae en la primera)

Corroboration (Glaser, Black & Benton 1997): table (2) 'Chichicapan tone and stress', pp. 11-12; 'the initial nucleus of a root will reduce (in stress and/or glottalization) if the root is not the final root in the word', p. 25 (exx. 3562.tone: Tone language with stress as a separate property. Smith Stark 2007 (same example (5)) lists three tones, 'grave (sin marca), ascendente (´) y descendente (^)', written on the tone-bearing vowel, and four laryngealization types 'V, V7, VV', V'V', beside the 'acento de intensidad'. Glaser, Black & Benton 1997 table (2) 'Chichicapan tone and stress' encodes tone, stress and glottalization jointly in the vowel letters ('v rising tone with stress', 'vh low tone with stress', 'vv rising tone on long vowel', 'vvh high falling tone on long vowel'...). Benton 1987 (SIL-Mexico Workpapers 9, fn. p. 72) lists six tones (low, high, low-rising, high-rising, low-falling, high-falling). No source gives a tone-based stress rule; stress is placed morphologically.

No word stress is described; the author uses 'tone' explicitly 'as opposed to accent'.

Two basic tones H and L (whether H vs L or H vs Ø left open); F only as H on a heavy penultimate syllable utterance-finally, never on the antepenult or the final syllable (final syllables are monomoraic); High Tone Anticipation shifts a final or penultimate H one syllable left in isolation (Rukiga anticipates the penultimate H too, unlike Runyankore); utterance-final L lowering (declination). Sister variety Runyankore (Hyman 2020 SPiL Plus 62, p. 53): privative /H/ vs Ø with Final High Retraction; also does not discuss stress.

3564.prule: Fixed final stress: stress (more emphasis, loudness) falls on the last syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive and independent of the three-way lexical tone; the examples show final stress on both low-toned (guli, selatax) and high-toned (seqí, qá'áb) final syllables, and on possessed nouns with prefixes (seqí 'my feet', selatax 'palm of my hand').

3564.quote: 1. Stress Stress occurs on the last syllable of the word. It is manifested by having more emphasis, loudness, etc. In the following words, stress is on the last syllable: qá'áb 'sack', seqí 'my feet', guli 'skunk', dadáben 'medicine', selatax 'palm of my hand'. 2. Tone contrasts and allotones In Chilcotin there is a contrast of three tones: high versus low versus a downgliding contour. In words of two syllables there are the following patterns: low-low, low-high, high-low, high-high, high-contour and low-contour.

3564.exq_: Stress occurs on the last syllable of the word. It is manifested by having more emphasis, loudness, etc.
3564.tone: The source is primarily a tone description: three tones, high vs low vs a downgliding contour (contour only word-final; section 3c), with progressive tone sandhi (words with a final high may raise a following low; words with a final contour may lower a following high; section 3). Stress is treated in a separate one-paragraph section as a property distinct from tone (loudness/emphasis on the final syllable, on low- as well as high-toned finals). The other reachable descriptions (Krauss 1975 section 1.4; Cook 2013 Introduction section 0.2.1; Ham 2008 p. 13; Bird & Onosson 2023 p. 837) describe Chilcotin as a two-tone language (marked high vs unmarked low, with high-tone spread and tone reversal) and say nothing about stress.

Swanton 1900: 207 adds the only general tendency, 'a marked disinclination to accent the ultima', and notes that a or E is inserted purely to carry the accent when it is thrown forward.

3568.tone: Sharma labels the contrast 'Tone/stress' without deciding between them; the only evidence is two monosyllabic pairs (/ghà/ grass: /gha/ wound; /né/ carry: /ne/ river) with grave/acute marks, which in monosyllables can only be a pitch contrast, so a tone or pitch accent reading (Western-Pahari-type tone) is the live alternative. 3570.dq: Jaker's subjective impression is that where there is more than one stress in a prosodic word, the rightmost stress is the primary stress. [p. 18] ... a high–low tone pattern will result in a trochee in two-syllable words. [p. 17]
3570.dloc: §4 pp. 17–18 (primary vs secondary stress in the prosodic word; two-syllable words)
3570.heavy: Heavy = syllable with a long vowel, or a closed syllable whose coda is moraic: 'we assume that word-final codas (which are also stem-final) are moraic, whereas most codas in prefixes are not moraic, with two exceptions' (p. 12); 'all consonants are moraic word-finally... the coda consonants of the first-person-plural prefix hít and the second-person-plural prefix uh also count as moraic, whereas all other coda consonants in prefixes count as non-moraic' (p. 14); 'The coda consonant ɬ does not add coda weight in (13c) and (13d)' (p. 11); 'all stems (the final syllable) are obligatorily heavy (Jaker and Cardinal 2020: 73)' (p. 16).
3570.dflt: Not exemplified: the source states that all stems are obligatorily heavy and word-final (p. 16), so no all-light word occurs in the verb data. By the stated rule, light syllables pair from the left into (L ˈL) iambs, i.e. stress on even-numbered syllables from the left, with a final light syllable extrametrical (cf. (ja.ˈneɬ)(ˈthiː) where the first foot is (L ˈL)).
3570.prule: Iterative left-to-right quantity-sensitive iambic footing: every heavy syllable heads a foot; a light syllable forms an iamb with the heavy or light syllable to its immediate right ((L ˈH), (L ˈL)); word-final light syllables are extrametrical. Tone overrides weight: high tone attracts stress, so an initial H–L sequence gives a trochee and a low-toned syllable after a high-toned one is unstressed. Where a word has more than one stress, the rightmost is primary (Jaker's impression, p. 18; not acoustically confirmed, fn. 4). Examples (13): (he.ˈtãː) 'he/she drinks', (ˈheː)(ˈtãː) 'they drink', (ja.ˈneɬ)(ˈthiː) 'you (sg.) speak', (ˈthaː)ɣe 'three'; (21c) (ˈhí.tãː) 'we drink'; (22c) (he.ˈné)kheː 'they have sat down'; (22e) (ˈʃé.he)(ˈkhĩː) 'they (du.) eat'.
3570.srule: Iterative footing: every foot head of the left-to-right quantity-sensitive iambic parse is stressed and the rightmost stress is (impressionistically) primary, so secondary stresses fall on each non-final foot head — every non-final heavy syllable, the second syllable of each (L L)/(L H) iamb from the left edge, and an initial H-toned syllable before a L tone — e.g. (ˈheː)(ˈtãː), (ja.ˈneɬ)(ˈthiː), (ˈʃé.he)(ˈkhĩː), (ˈháú)(te.ˈnes)(ˈthən); no acoustic difference between primary and secondary stress was found (fn. 4).

If we put aside the role of tone, the interaction between quantity and iambic feet in Tetsǫ́t’ıné is typologically normal for an iambic system (cf. Hayes 1995). Thus, every heavy syllable constitutes the head of a foot. Light syllables can form a foot together with a heavy syllable to their immediate right, or else two light syllables can also form a foot. This is illustrated in the examples in (13). Here, H and L refer to heavy and light syllables, respectively, rather than tones. The coda co…

3570.tone: Tetsǫ́t’ıné has four contrastive tones (High, Low, Rising, Falling; abstract p. 1) and contrastive vowel length, alongside 'a phonologically active stress system' (p. 18). High tone attracts stress (TSP); a low-toned syllable following a high-toned one is unstressed (p. 17). In a minority of cases stress conditions vowel-length transfer and tone movement (§3.4.1–3.4.3). Acoustically duration is the primary stress correlate, intensity secondary, F0 shows no significant effect (pp. 1, 36). Older sources describe tone only: Legoff 1889 pp. 10–11 (each word has its 'note ou ton'), Petitot 1876; Goddard 1912 p. 83 notes pitch differences with no within-syllable contour.

tn.quote: The first general fact to establish is that the inventory of tonal contrasts depends both on position (stems versus prefixes) and vowel length (short versus long). Specifically, in prefixes, short vowels contrast two tones (high and low), whereas long vowels contrast four tones (high, low, rising and falling). In stems, on the other hand, there are only two tones, high or low, regardless of whether the vowel is long (full) or short (reduced). ... in both stems and prefixes, the number of possible tonal specifications is equal to the number of vocalic root nodes.

dfl.q: Existe una cierta regularidad de acentuación ... 1) se acentúa Ia última (sin acento escrito) en palabras terminadas en r, s (z), y, s ... (hay bastantes excepciones ...). 2) se acentúa la penúltima, si la palabra (terminando en una vocal) no tiene otro acento: ãsamuka, poftii etc . 3) todas las palabras no pertenecientes a estas dos clases reciben el acento escrito: tapi, izaí, etc .

3575.prule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root by default; if the root has a syllable with two vowels (a diphthong, iV/uV, or an interrupted vowel V'V) or a vowel plus nasal coda, that syllable is stressed instead, wherever it sits in the root; in compounds the second root carries the stress by the same rules. Words whose stress is off-rule exist and are written with an accent when a minimal pair exists (beló 'cueva' vs belo 'estrella'; guibá 'cielo' vs guiba 'fierro').

3576.prule: No word-stress placement rule is stated. The author's 'stress' (svarbhar / bhar / bharank) is attached to particular vowels, not to a position: (i) a word-final reduced nasal schwa written a+halant+anusvara (< Gujarati neuter -um: ketlum > k-tram, jetlum > j-tram, atlum > a-tram, kahevum > k-vanam, calvum > c-anvanam) 'is not pronounced clearly/openly; its stress passes to the preceding vowel'; (ii) an 'additional stressed vowel' a-with-dot-below, pronounced between Gujarati a and o, word-initial in all six examples (p. 131: a-dot-ksar 'letter', a-dot-kan 'intelligence/advice', a-dot-rvan 'girl accompanying a bride', a-dot-ltam 'iron blade fixed to a goad'; p. 132: a-dot-dagvi 'near', a-dot-phano 'opium'), 'spoken with stress placed on a-dot'; (iii) 'in the pronunciation of intham [from here] stress is placed on tham' (final syllable). Initial, penultimate and final are thus each claimed for different words, and the proposed notation (mark on the last letter of the word, or under an initial letter when needed) presupposes that position varies by word. Sec. 4.16 p. 177 adds only that 'bharank-vala' (stressed) sounds occur in Chaudhari, Gamit and Kunkna with u-, a-, a(schwa)- and e-final words (table 4.56: mitham, khhanam, ekatham; 'in Kunkna no bharank is seen here'), 'especially in words used for the neuter or for abstracts'.

3577.prule: Tone language: two basic tones, high and low (H written with acute, L unmarked or grave, long vowels with circumflex, after Fernandes & Ntondo 2002); tonal minimal pair tanga/tangá 'read/reads'. The only accent statement is partial and orthographic: when a word ends in two vowels they form two syllables and the first (i.e. the penult) is 'always accented'; the glides w/y are written to move the accent onto the following vowel (ku-fua vs ku-fw-a 'to die', limbia vs y-im-by-a 'pot'). No general stress rule is stated for the language, and 'acento/acentuada' is also the author's word for the acute tone mark, so the remark is ambiguous between stress and tone. No reachable secondary source states a Chokwe stress rule (the StressTyp 'penultimate syllable of the stem' entry is Luvale's).

tn.quote: Outra particularidade da língua Cokwe está relacionada com o sistema tonal desta língua que apresenta uma articulação tonal baseada em dois tons de base: tom alto e tom baixo. Segundo FERNANDES e NTONDO (2002), na língua Cokwe, os tons altos são grafados com um acento agudo (´), os tons baixos com um acento grave (`) ... O tom baixo não é marcado; a ausência de notação tonal sobre uma vogal significa que esta é de tom baixo, por exemplo: [ngálò]-ngálo (cesto) ... A distinção entre o tom alto e o tom baixo foi estabelecido a partir dos pares mínimos tonais do tipo: [kú] - tanga/tangá (ler/lê).
tn.translation: Another particularity of Cokwe concerns its tonal system, which shows a tonal articulation based on two basic tones: high tone and low tone. According to Fernandes and Ntondo (2002), in Cokwe high tones are written with an acute accent, low tones with a grave accent ... Low tone is not marked; the absence of tone notation over a vowel means it is low-toned, e.g. [ngálò]-ngálo (basket) ... The distinction between high and low tone was established from tonal minimal pairs of the type [kú] - tanga/tangá (to read/reads).

tn.note: Two level tones, high and low, on every vowel; circumflex long vowels = high plus non-lowered tone; notation after Fernandes & Ntondo 2002; no downstep; a vague remark on final-vowel 'accent' (p. 40). 3578.tone: The 1902 sketch describes no tone, pitch or intonation anywhere (a full-text search of the whole book finds only 'to pitch' in the dictionary); its 'tonic accent' is the pre-tonal-era label for the Southern Bantu penultimate length/stress prominence. Chopi (Bantu S61) is tonal by the title of Bailey 1976 'Copi phonology and morphotonology' (unreached) and by Gowlett 2003 sec. 3.7 (two-tone Zone S); Gowlett 2003 sec. 3.6 states zone-wide 'a penultimate length-stress feature which signals the end of a phrase or sentence in declarative sentences. This accent is not used in interrogative and exclamatory sentences.' A modern Chopi-proper source would very likely yield a tonal system with phrase-final penultimate lengthening rather than a bare fixed-stress rule.

tn.quote: Zone S languages have a two-tone system, or a system in which some syllables are accented (by a High tone) while other syllables are unaccented. High tones may spread rightwards to unaccented (Low-toned) syllables under certain circumstances. In general each syllable carries only one tone (High or Low), but some syllables are bimoric – they bear High-High, Low-Low, Rising (Low-High) or Falling (High-Low) tones. Probably all Zone S languages, with the exception of Lozi, have tonal downstep ... In Copi, murmured consonants act as depressors, lowering the onset of a following High.

3579.prule: Lexical (contrastive, unpredictable) stress: any syllable of the phonological word may be stressed, more than one syllable may carry stress, and the only constraint is that every P-word contains at least one stressed syllable; minimal pairs kúba 'stick' vs kubá 'bamboo type'. Swick lists 3 patterns for disyllables, 7 for trisyllables and 10 for four-syllable words (sec. 3.1 p. 38). No default position and no weight condition is stated.
3579.srule: No primary/secondary ranking: a word may carry more than one equal lexical stress, each on a lexically specified syllable (dúdí, nímbígá, yágóri, amámó, énugú, kábúóri) -- Swick's 'multiple stress hypothesis'. No rhythmic or predictable secondary stress is described; one lexical stress may be promoted to an emphatic nucleus only at pause-group (phrase) level.

3583.prule: Word accent on the stem (root) syllable; in unprefixed native words this is the first syllable (khriage, prìdige, lùstegarste). Words with an unstressed prefix (ge-, dar-) stress the stem, i.e. the second syllable (gevallt, darzürnt). Romance loans keep non-initial stress and are written with an accent mark (botù, konfì, frenàrn, fadìge).

3584.prule: No word-stress rule. The source treats Cinene as a two-tone (H/L) language and marks tone on every word of its wordlist (H unmarked, L with grave), but says the contrastive function of tone has not yet been established and its functional load appears small. 'Stress phenomena' (강세 현상) are said to appear only in some morpho-syntactic environments, the one example being the plural suffix {-´xà}, and to be uncommon overall. In the plural examples (waɣà > waɣa-xà, udà > uda-xà, ɬà > ɬa-xà) the stem-final L vowel surfaces unmarked (= H) before -xà; the author himself calls this 강세 (stress) and writes the suffix with a preceding acute, a mark outside his stated tone convention, so reading it as a floating-H tonal raising rather than a stress is the compilers' inference. Either way no positional stress rule is stated.

3584.tone: Tone: every word in the 110-item comparative wordlist (pp. 132-139; Swadesh 100 plus additions, p. 129) and in the elicited sentences is tone-marked, H unmarked and L marked with a grave (note at the foot of p. 132: 고성조는 별도로 표시하지 않고 (/a/) 저성조만 표시함 (/à/)); the consonant and vowel inventories rest on some 650 lexical items (p. 139). The author says the tone marking is simply what he heard, that the H/L pitch difference is less audible than in Hausa or Yoruba, that no environments where tone is contrastive have yet been found, and that the functional load of tone appears small in Cinene, Glavda and Guduf alike (pp. 140-141). Kim 2002 (same author, classification paper) states generically that Chadic languages are tone languages. Stress/accent: no positional rule; 'stress phenomena' only in some morpho-syntactic environments, e.g. the plural suffix {-´xà}, and uncommon overall; in the plural examples on p. 145 the stem-final L vowel surfaces unmarked (H) before -xà (waɣà > waɣa-xà); the author calls this 강세, and a floating-H tonal reading is the compilers' inference. Vowel length: H-toned vowels sometimes slightly long, but length not distinctive.

3585.prule: No word-stress rule stated. Kambari (explicitly including Agwara Kambari = Cishingini) is described as a tone language with two level lexical tones (H, L) carrying a very small semantic load; noun melodies LL/HL/LH and LLL/LHL/LHH/HLL/HHH, imperative verbs nearly always LH; Agwara has under 20 minimal tone pairs and leaves tone unmarked in the orthography. 3585.tone: Source treats prosody only as tone: 'Kambari utilizes two level lexical tones' (p. 61); lexical tone load 'very small' (p. 61), 'burden of comprehension based on tone contrast is slight' (p. 98); 'There are no semantic elements represented by tone alone' (p. 63); Agwara-specific: 'a small number of minimal tone pairs (under 20)' (p. 192), tone unmarked in the Agwara orthography. Grammatical tone: first syllable of a verb is always H after Set 2 subject pronouns (p. 63). A full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/rhythm/intonation finds only 'Dawson stresses' (verb), 'acute accent mark' (tone diacritic), 'more prominent' (NCM vs pronoun salience) and the heading 'Unstressed /u/' in the AUNA Kambari appendix (p. 200: root-final vowel replaced by /u/ before a suffix 'does not receive the same length and "importance" as the same vowel in other positions'), a segmental-reduction note for Tsikimba (kdl), not a word-stress rule for Agwara. No statement of word stress or accent anywhere.
